editorial:
Charlie Chaplin wrote, produced, and directed this three-reel silent comedy, released April 14, 1918, as the first film under his landmark $1 million contract with First National Pictures Inc. Chaplin registered the copyright in his own name that April; under the 1909 Copyright Act the initial 28-year term ran to 1946, and even a timely renewal could have extended protection only to 1974. Because no US law revives expired domestic copyrights, the silent print has been in the public domain since the mid-1970s. The story is also Chaplin's own original work with no underlying source to track.

The live rights trap is the score. The 1918 original was exhibited with varying live accompaniment and had no fixed synchronized track. In 1959 Chaplin composed a new orchestral score (with Eric James as musical associate) for The Chaplin Revue; conductor Timothy Brock later restored that score for live performance in 2003 under commission from Roy Export Company S.A.S., which holds the score copyright. A 2026 MoMA 4K reconstructionâ€”made at Cineric laboratory under Association Chaplin and Roy Export Company Establishmentâ€”adds a further layer of protected authorship in the restoration itself. Every commercial release through Criterion, MK2, or the official Chaplin channel carries one or both protected layers. The Archive.org copy uploaded in 2024 includes a musical track whose copyright status should be confirmed independently before any broadcast or distribution use.
faq: Is the film footage itself free to use in the US?

The silent print is in the public domain by copyright term expiry â€” Chaplin registered the copyright in April 1918, and the 56-year maximum under the 1909 Act expired no later than 1974. Confirm that your source copy does not carry the 1959 Chaplin orchestral score (copyrighted by Roy Export Company S.A.S.) or originate from the 2026 MoMA restoration, both of which are separately protected.
Can I use the version on the Criterion Channel or other commercial streaming platforms?

No. Those versions use the 2026 MoMA 4K restoration and/or the 1959 Chaplin score, both under Roy Export Company copyright. Source your copy from an archive that can confirm it carries only a public-domain or royalty-free musical accompaniment, or license the score separately from Roy Export S.A.S.
